title.narrative: DRA_ACM Indonesia Flood Response 2025-6

description.narrative: 15000 people (3750HH) in the 3 most affected districts (Aceh Tamiang, East Aceh, North Aceh)

Save the Children implements an integrated WASH, Health, and Child Protection (CP) response, mainstreaming protection, for 15000 people (3750HH) in the 3 most affected districts (Aceh Tamiang, East Aceh, North Aceh), building on complementary strengths of SC and Geutanyoe Foundation (LP), ensuring rapid, locally grounded and technically sound delivery. It aligns with WASH SPHERE Standards; WHO guidelines for emergency health services; CP Minimum Standards; and the CaLP Good Practice Guidelines for CfW. WASH: we will provide portable water treatment units (600HH) and emergency water trucking (3750HH); distribute hygiene (1000HH) and emergency latrine (600HH) kits; conduct hygiene promotion (3500 people); provide sanitation rehabilitation in public facilities (60 units); and conduct CfW for villages and houses cleanup (1142 head of HH) based on 210000 IDR per day per person for 3 days. Staff report 65% of markets are active in areas removed from the river basin. Existing MoU with National Post Office will be utilized. Health: we will operate MHCs in 10 areas for 10 days to reach 3000 people with essential primary healthcare, disease prevention and health education. MHCs will include PSS for 1500 people. Minor rehabilitation will be done in 12 damaged health facilities in 3 districts. CP: we will identify CP cases, provide case management (CM) support for 65 children, strengthen referral mechanisms within existing community and district-level CP systems. Based on confidentially and resources, CM cases will either be handled by SC or referred to local authorities with continuous monitoring until resolution. SC has aligned proposed activities with other DRA partners who provide MPCA, establish public kitchens and promote infant and young child feeding, as well as provide PSS. SC will complement Plan in East Aceh, and Oxfam in north Aceh. We will coordinate closely with BNPB, subnational governments, the military and line ministries to align with national response strategies.

Sectoral needs assessments conducted by Save the Children Indonesia (SC) and local partner, Geutanyoe Foundation (Guetanyoe) in Aceh Tamiang, East Aceh and North Aceh, complemented by findings from National Disaster Management Agency (BNPB) and other local partners inform the design of the response. These reveal severe disruption to access safe water and sanitation, health and protection services. Flooding has contaminated wells and surface water sources, forcing communities to rely on unsafe alternatives for drinking and household (HH) use. Large amounts of debris and waste have accumulated, creating unsanitary conditions and health risks. There is an acute shortage of hygiene items (ie. soap, sanitary pads) leaving families unable to maintain basic cleanliness and increasing the risk of waterborne and hygiene-related diseases, which is worsened by the collapse of WASH infrastructure, with many latrines damaged or submerged. There is overflow, contamination, and open defecation in temporary shelters. Communities express a strong need for organized cleaning and waste management efforts, which will help restore safe living environments and provide short-term income opportunities if done via cash-for-work (CfW). As of 11 Dec, BNPB reports that 153 health facilities are damaged in Aceh, which limits access to essential primary health care. SC and its partners have deployed mobile health clinics (MHC) in 4 Aceh Tamiang locations, however additional units are urgently needed to reach remote, flood-isolated villages and deliver primary health care incl. psychosocial support (PSS). Strengthening of community-based protection systems is needed to identify, refer, and support children at risk of abuse, neglect, or exploitation. Children face heightened risks of abuse, neglect, exploitation and sexual-gender based violence (SGBV) in overcrowded shelters as a result of disrupted family structures and limited supervision.
